opus-5.5.text:
That's the question I think about most. The vision is a loop with two halves that feed each other: a conjecturer and a prover.

Today most of the field treats theorem proving as "here's a statement, go prove it." That's important, but it's only half of what mathematicians do. The other half, arguably the more creative half, is deciding what's worth proving: spotting patterns, generalizing, asking "what if I drop this hypothesis?" For a system to keep getting better, it can't depend on humans to hand it an endless supply of good problems. It has to generate its own.

So the conjecturer proposes statements. Some are conjectures about known objects, some are lemmas the system suspects it needs, some are variations on things it has already proven. The prover then works on them in a formal language like Lean. Formal verification is what makes the whole loop trustworthy. Every proof is checked by the kernel, so there's no hallucination problem. A proof either compiles or it doesn't. That gives you a perfectly clean reward signal, which is rare in AI.

Then the outputs feed back in. Successful proofs become training data, and verified lemmas join a growing library the prover can reuse. Failed attempts are informative too. If something resists proof, maybe it's false, so you look for a counterexample. Maybe it's true but needs a missing intermediate result, which becomes a new conjecture. The system is building its own curriculum.

The subtle part is keeping the conjecturer honest about what's interesting. It's easy to generate millions of trivially true or trivially false statements, and that teaches you nothing. You want conjectures right at the edge of the prover's ability: hard enough to stretch it, not so hard they're hopeless. You also want some taste. Does this statement connect to other things? Does it compress a lot of special cases? Would a mathematician care? Building that sense of mathematical taste is one of the deepest research problems we have.

If the loop works, you get something like self-play in games, except the game is open-ended. In Go the board is fixed. Mathematics keeps expanding as you explore it. That's what excites me. The ceiling isn't set by human data, because the system is generating and verifying new mathematics itself.

Ultimately I see it as a collaborator for mathematicians, not a replacement. It can take on the enormous amount of verification and exploration, so people can spend more time on the questions that need human intuition and vision.

r001.rationale: It describes a conjecturer and prover feeding into each other, with proof outcomes generating further conjectures.

r002.rationale: It says successful proofs become training data and verified lemmas join a growing library the prover can reuse.

r003.rationale: It identifies kernel-checked proofs and the clean compile-or-not reward signal as a feature that is rare in AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, mathematics has always advanced through a loop between two activities: coming up with the right questions, and then answering them. Historically, a prover like ours was only on the second half of that loop. You hand it a formal statement, it searches for a proof, and that's the end. What we're trying to build with Axiom is a system that closes the loop itself.

So concretely, the prover doesn't just sit and wait for a human to feed it a conjecture. It looks at the body of mathematics it already has access to, formalized in Lean, and it starts proposing new statements. Some of these are small lemmas, some are generalizations of things it just proved, some are analogies pulled from a different area. Then it tries to prove them. And here's the key thing: because everything is formally verified, every success is a hard, incorruptible signal. There's no hallucination problem at the output end. Either the proof type-checks or it doesn't.

That gives you a very clean training signal. Every proved conjecture becomes new training data, and it also becomes a new tool in the library that makes the next, harder conjecture reachable. So the system is effectively building its own curriculum. The conjectures it generates today are ones that are just beyond its current ability, and once it can prove them, the frontier moves.

The subtle part, and honestly the part I find most interesting, is that not all true statements are worth proving. Mathematics is full of trivially true things. So a big portion of the work is teaching the system taste: which conjectures are interesting, which ones unlock other results, which ones a human mathematician would actually care about. We measure that partly by downstream utility, meaning does proving this lemma make other open problems easier, and partly by learning from how mathematicians themselves judge significance.

My longer-term hope is that this turns into something like a self-improving research mathematician. Not replacing people, but running the exploratory, grinding part of the loop at a scale and speed no human department could, and surfacing the genuinely surprising results to humans who can then decide where to point it next.

r001.rationale: The response describes Axiom proposing conjectures, proving them, and using each proved conjecture to make harder conjectures reachable, forming a reinforcing cycle.

r002.rationale: It says proved conjectures become both new training data and tools in the library for reaching later conjectures.

r003.rationale: It presents formal verification as a hard, reliable signal—proofs either type-check or do not—and connects that signal to training and self-improvement.

astra-6.text:
I envision a loop where Axiom Prover can propose conjectures, try to prove them, and learn from that process. Rather than only solving problems we give it, it would start generating some of its own training tasks.

The interesting challenge is choosing good conjectures. If they’re too easy, it doesn’t learn much; if they’re far beyond its capabilities, it may make no progress. You want conjectures that stretch what it can do, especially ones that lead to useful intermediate lemmas. A proof assistant can check whether a proof is correct, giving us a reliable signal for successful attempts.

But correctness alone doesn’t tell you whether a conjecture is interesting. So I think an important part of self-improvement is learning which questions are worth asking—which results unlock other results. The vision is for conjecture-making and proving to reinforce each other: better conjectures create better learning opportunities, and stronger proving capabilities let the system explore deeper mathematics.

r001.rationale: It says conjecture-making and proving should reinforce each other, with better conjectures creating learning opportunities and stronger proving enabling deeper exploration.

r002.rationale: It mentions useful intermediate lemmas and results that unlock other results, but does not clearly propose reusing results Axiom Prover has already proved to improve itself.

r003.rationale: It identifies proof checking as a reliable correctness signal for successful attempts in the self-improvement loop, supporting mathematics as a testbed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a loop between proposing something interesting and learning from the attempt to prove it. Axiom Prover could make a conjecture, try to construct a proof, and use what happens to guide its next step. If it succeeds, that result might become a useful lemma for a harder problem. If it gets stuck, it might need a different intermediate claim, or the conjecture itself might need to change.

The challenge is choosing conjectures that are productive. You don’t want a system that generates endless statements that are easy to prove but don’t lead anywhere. You want it to identify questions that help build a richer mathematical theory.

And I’d distinguish checking a proof from improving the model. A verified proof gives you a reliable result, but turning that experience into better conjectures and better proof strategies requires a learning process. The vision is for those pieces to reinforce each other: better conjectures lead to useful proofs, and those proofs help the system ask better questions.

r001.rationale: It describes conjectures leading to proofs and proof outcomes guiding better conjectures and strategies, forming a reinforcing cycle.

r002.rationale: It says a proved result could become a useful lemma for a harder problem and that proofs can help the system ask better questions.

r003.rationale: It calls a verified proof reliable, but does not identify mathematics’ verification signals as a reason it can serve as a testbed for AI self-improvement.
